items.prompt: Per L2, what's the actual test this unit uses to distinguish "white" (legitimate) influence-building from other forms of politics?
choices: Whether the person doing it has any self-interested motive at all
Whether the mechanism would still work, undamaged, if the other person fully understood exactly what was being done and why — legitimate mechanisms don't depend on concealment to function
Whether the action involves any strategic thinking about relationships
Whether the action is done in public versus in private
items.explanation: The test is deliberately mechanical: a genuine pattern of help works the same whether or not it's explicitly named, while a manipulation tactic typically stops working once it's called out — that's the actual dividing line, not the mere presence of strategy or self-interest.

items.prompt: Per L2's comparison table, why does help given consistently with no immediate ask build more durable trust than help given with an explicit "in exchange for X"?
choices: It doesn't — both approaches build identical trust

The explicit-exchange version settles a specific transaction and builds no ongoing goodwill; help given with no immediate ask accumulates as a felt, unspecified goodwill that the other person tends to reciprocate on their own initiative later
Because explicit exchanges are always dishonest
Because unconditional help is required by most corporate codes of conduct
items.explanation: The mechanism depends specifically on the help not being tightly coupled to an immediate ask — that's what makes it feel like goodwill rather than a transaction, and what makes people repay it voluntarily rather than feeling an exact debt has been settled.

items.prompt: Per L2, is "visibility" (sharing a postmortem, presenting results) the same thing as exaggerating or inflating your work's importance?
choices: Yes — any deliberate effort to be seen is inherently exaggeration
No — visibility means making real, accurate work legible to people who'd otherwise never encounter it; it requires no inflation, just the separate step of actually communicating what was true anyway
Yes, because good work should speak for itself without any communication effort
No, but only if the work is presented anonymously
items.explanation: L2 explicitly separates these: visibility is about legibility, not embellishment. Good work that's never communicated to anyone outside the immediate team builds skill but not influence, purely because nobody positioned to extend trust based on it ever encounters it.

items.prompt: In L3, Engineer B never said anything untrue or manipulative in any individual conversation, yet the outreach still read as "networking with an agenda." What actually caused that impression, per L3?
choices: B's colleagues were simply too cynical to trust genuine outreach

The timing and compression — B's relationship-building was concentrated into a single month explicitly ahead of an ask, which reads as transactional regardless of individual honesty, unlike Engineer A's pattern spread genuinely across the whole year with no immediate payoff attached
B used more formal language than Engineer A
B's proposal was technically worse than Engineer A's, which colored the reception
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that B's individual actions weren't dishonest — the difference was entirely about pattern and timing. Reciprocity specifically depends on not being tightly coupled to an immediate, visible payoff, which is exactly what B's compressed outreach violated.

items.prompt: Per L3's third failure mode, does being strategically aware that helping colleagues builds trust and influence over time make Engineer A's behavior less "genuine"?
choices: Yes — any awareness of the strategic value of an action makes it manipulative by definition

No — genuine and strategic aren't opposites; the transparency test isn't about having zero self-interested awareness, it's about whether the mechanism requires the other person NOT understanding what's happening
Yes, but only if the person explicitly plans out each interaction in advance
No, because strategic thinking is impossible to detect from outside anyway
items.explanation: L3 directly addresses this: Engineer A plausibly understood the broader value of the pattern of behavior, and that doesn't disqualify it as legitimate — the test remains whether it would survive being explained aloud, which A's pattern does and B's compressed, ask-adjacent version doesn't as cleanly.
